text: An image should be built once and promoted unchanged across environments, but dev, staging, and production almost always need different settings. Baking those differences into the image means rebuilding per environment, which defeats the point. This lesson covers the two Kubernetes objects that solve it instead: ConfigMaps and Secrets.

A ConfigMap is just a bucket of key-value pairs, stored as a real cluster object instead of a file sitting next to your code. You can create one from literal values, from a file, or as YAML you'd commit to version control. Whichever way you create it, the application image itself never has to change between environments — only the ConfigMap it's pointed at does.

A Pod consumes either object one of two ways. As environment variables, through envFrom and configMapRef or secretRef, which injects every key directly into the container's environment. Or as a mounted file, which matters for configuration an application reads from disk rather than the environment, like an nginx config or an appsettings file.

Secrets have the identical shape and the identical consumption pattern as ConfigMaps — the real difference is intent and handling. They're meant for database passwords, API keys, and certificates, and kubectl treats them a little more carefully: describe won't print the full value, and stringData lets you author plaintext in YAML while Kubernetes base64-encodes it for storage on your behalf.

Be clear about what that base64 encoding actually buys you: nothing, from a security standpoint. It's an encoding, not encryption — anyone who can read the Secret object can decode the value back to plaintext in one command. Real protection comes from RBAC restricting who can read Secrets at all, and from encrypting etcd at rest, not from the encoding itself.

ConfigMaps and Secrets both get injected at runtime, so the image stays identical everywhere it runs. Next lesson puts the whole object hierarchy to work for real: a rolling update of a running Deployment, followed by a rollback with kubectl when the new version turns out to be broken.
